full_judgment:
6. Mr. BK Das, learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-petitioner, submits that according to the plaintiff himself, defendant-petitioner was let out with the suit premises on stipulation of payment of Taka 800.00 as monthly rent to be paid on the following month according to Bengali calendar and that later with effect from 1396 BS increased Taka 1000.00 per month and that the defendant paid rent according to Bengali calendar month but the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act (Exhibit 5) was issued on 23-6-1993 asking the defendant to vacate the suit premises within 15 days from the date of receipt of the notice in question. He therefore submits that the notice being not given with reference to Bengali calendar month and also being not issued terminating the tenancy with the expiry of Bengali month the said notice is not a valid notice in the eye of law and, as such, in the absence of valid notice, the plaintiff was not entitled to get a decree of ejectment, as sought for, by him against the defendant-petitioner. He then submits that the trial Court without considering this vital legal flaw passed the impugned judgment and, as such, the judgment is liable to be set aside. 

 8. It appears from paragraph 2 of the plaint filed by the plaintiff-opposite party that there was no written agreement between the parties as they happened to be dose relations and that defendant No.1 was inducted as a tenant in the suit premises on condition of payment of monthly rent at the rate of Taka 800.00 'per month to be paid on the following month according to Bengali calendar and that. from 1396 BS rent was increased to Taka 1,000.00 per month and that the defendant paid rent upto Aswin 1399 BS and that the plaintiff being in bonafide requirement of the suit premises and also defendant becoming a defaulter in payment of rent, was requested, to vacate the suit premises and pay arrear rents: From the aforesaid averment it appears that the plaintiff filed the suit against the defendant for his eviction referring to the tenancy made according to Bengali calendar and, as such, repeatedly used Bengali year and Bengali month in the plaint and so by all means it must be held that the tenancy between the plaintiff and the defendant was a tenancy according to Bengali calendar month.It appears that the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was admittedly issued, on 23-6-1993 and according to plaintiff it was received by the defendant on 4-7-1993. Here again, it appears that the notice does not contain any reference whatsoever to the date according to Bengali calendar. The notice was issued terminating the tenancy within 15 days from the date of receipt of the notice. On the plaintiffs own showing the notice being received by the defendant on 4-7-1993, it is needless to say, that the defendant was asked to vacate the suit premises within 15 days from 4-7-1993 i.e. by 19-7-1993. It appears from paragraph 4 of the plaint that pursuant to the purport of the notice terminating the tenancy by 19-7-1993, plaintiff on his own showing in the said paragraph 4 of the plaint asked the defendant to vacate the suit premises and hand over possession in favour of the plaintiff and that on the following clay i.e. on 20-7-93 the plaintiff approached the defendant for handing over possession of the suit premises and admittedly, according to the plaintiff, the cause of action thus arose on 20-7-1993 on the failure of the defendant to vacate the suit premises and hand over possession in favour of the plaintiff-opposite party. Learned Advocate appearing' for' the defendant-petitioner seriously challenged the validity of the notice issued under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, Section 106 of the Transfer or Property Act-runs as follows: 

 "106. In the absence of a contract or local law or usage to the contrary, a lease of immovable property for agricultural or manufacturing purposes shall be deemed to be a lease from year to year, terminable, on the part of either lessor or lessee, by six month's notice expiring with the end of a year of the tenancy; and a lease of immovable property of any other purpose shall be deemed to be a lease from month to month, terminable, on the part of either lessor or lessee, by fifteen day's notice expiring with the end of a month of the tenancy. 

 9. It appears from the above provision that in case of a monthly tenant the tenancy, can be terminated by 15 day's notice expiring with the end of a month of the tenancy. A notice as contemplated by law therefore should be a notice of 15 days expiring with the end of a month of the tenancy. In other words, the notice must contemplate the period of expiry of the tenancy with the month of the tenancy. In the Instant case it is already found that the notice was issued on 23-6-1993 which was received by the defendant on 4-7-1993 terminating his tenancy within 15 days from the date of receipt of the notice which being received on 4-7-1993 the tenancy thus expired on 19-7-1993 which cannot be regarded to be a notice expiring with the end of a month. Further, it has been provided therein that such notice is to be issued terminating tenancy by 15 day's notice expiring with the end of a month of the tenancy. On elaborate discussion made above and from the plaint itself it has already been noticed that the tenancy in question in the present suit was according to Bengali Calendar month and the instant notice therefore having no reference to the Bengali Calendar month the notice served upon the defendant cannot be regarded as a notice expiring tenancy with the end of a month of the tenancy. 

 10. Mr. BK Das, learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-petitioner, in this connection referred to the case of Seati Bibi vs Jogendra Nath reported in 57 Indian Clues (IC) 593. A plaintiff sought for ejectment of the defendant serving it notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. The defendant raised objection as to issuance of the legal notice. The learned Munsif framed an issue on the point but the learned Munsif came to a finding against the plaintiff on another issue and did not determine this issue. In appeal the learned District Judge upheld the order of the learned Munsif. The case reaching the High Court discussed the facts and found that the notice in question was issued on 28th December 1915. The notice directed defendant to vacate the house by 31-1-1916. The Court below found that the defendant was holding on a monthly tenant terminating on the 26th day of each successive month according to Hindu calendar. This finding being a finding of fact was regarded by the High Court Division to be binding upon him. In view of the discussion made above it appears that in order to be a valid notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act it would be issued terminating tenancy by 15 day's notice expiring firstly with the end of a month and secondly, with the end of a monthly tenancy. Thus the two essential ingredients being not complied with in the instant case while issuing notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, I am of the opinion that the notice is not a valid notice terminating the tenancy of the defendant. 

 "lease of immovable property is created under section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act and, as such, statutory notice must be given under section 106 of the Transfer of Properly Act for termination of tenancy. The landlord should comply both with the provisions of section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act and also with the provisions of the special enactment. The provisions of the Rent Control Ordinance are in addition to this section of notice under section 106 of the Transfer of property Act. There is nothing in the Ordinance which also absolves the landlord to serve a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. Unless the tenancy is determined by giving a notice as contemplated under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act no suit for ejectment of a monthly tenant can be filed."
